title: Depth-First Search

sections.heading: Problem Statement and Graph Model
sections.body:
Depth-first search (DFS) takes a graph $G = (V, E)$, directed or undirected, given by an adjacency-list representation: for every vertex $v$, the list $\mathrm{Adj}[v]$ holds its neighbors. For an undirected graph $|\mathrm{Adj}[v]| = \deg(v)$, and by the handshaking lemma $\sum_{v \in V} \deg(v) = 2|E|$, so adjacency lists use $\Theta(V+E)$ storage — the sparse representation DFS is written against, as opposed to the $\Theta(V^2)$ adjacency matrix.

DFS produces a depth-first forest: one depth-first tree rooted at each vertex that starts a new search. For every vertex it records a predecessor $\pi[v]$, a discovery time $d[v]$ and a finish time $f[v]$, both timestamps drawn from one global clock shared by the whole forest and incremented exactly $2|V|$ times in total. It also classifies every edge of $G$ as a tree, back, forward or cross edge. The model of computation is the standard RAM model with adjacency lists; cost is counted in vertex visits and edge-list scans, not comparisons.

sections.heading: The Algorithm
sections.body:
DFS colors each vertex white (undiscovered), gray (discovered, still has white neighbors to explore — on the current root-to-frontier path) or black (finished, entire subtree explored):

```
DFS(G):
  for each u in G.V: color[u] = WHITE; pi[u] = NIL
  time = 0
  for each u in G.V:
    if color[u] == WHITE: DFS-VISIT(G, u)

DFS-VISIT(G, u):
  time = time + 1; d[u] = time; color[u] = GRAY
  for each v in Adj[u]:
    if color[v] == WHITE:
      pi[v] = u; DFS-VISIT(G, v)
  color[u] = BLACK; time = time + 1; f[u] = time
```

The outer loop guarantees every vertex is visited even when $G$ is disconnected (or, for a digraph, not reachable from a single source), producing a forest rather than a single tree. Because a vertex turns gray exactly once and black exactly once, and the clock is shared, $d$ and $f$ give each vertex two distinct integers in $\{1, \dots, 2|V|\}$. The recursion is a call stack in the literal sense: a fully iterative rewrite with an explicit stack of (vertex, adjacency-list iterator) pairs computes the identical $d$, $f$ and $\pi$ values and is what production code without tail-call guarantees should use on deep graphs.

sections.heading: Correctness: the Parenthesis and White-Path Theorems
sections.body:
**Parenthesis theorem.** For any two vertices $u, v$, exactly one holds: the intervals $[d[u], f[u]]$ and $[d[v], f[v]]$ are disjoint and neither is an ancestor of the other; or $[d[u],f[u]] \subset [d[v],f[v]]$ and $u$ is a descendant of $v$; or $[d[v],f[v]] \subset [d[u],f[u]]$ and $v$ is a descendant of $u$. Sketch: assume $d[u] < d[v]$. If $v$ is discovered before $u$ finishes ($d[v] < f[u]$), $v$ was reached from inside $u$'s call and, because calls nest like a stack, $v$ must also finish before $u$ does, giving containment. Otherwise $d[v] > f[u]$ and the intervals are disjoint. Writing "(" at $d[v]$ and ")" at $f[v]$ for every vertex therefore always produces a correctly nested (balanced) parenthesization — the theorem's name.

**White-path theorem.** $v$ is a descendant of $u$ in the depth-first forest iff, at time $d[u]$, there is a path from $u$ to $v$ using only white vertices (aside from $u$ itself). ($\Rightarrow$) The tree path from $u$ to $v$ is traced by nested calls, and a vertex turns gray only the instant its own call starts, so every vertex on that path is still white just before it is reached. ($\Leftarrow$) Induct along the white path: its first edge leads to a white vertex still in $\mathrm{Adj}[u]$ when $u$'s loop reaches it (nothing else could have colored it, since no other call can run while $u$'s frame is active), so DFS-VISIT recurses into it and the argument repeats one edge at a time.

sections.heading: Edge Classification and Cycle Detection
sections.body:
Classify edge $(u,v)$ by the color of $v$ at the moment $u$'s adjacency list scans it: white → **tree edge** ($v$ becomes $u$'s child); gray → **back edge** ($v$ is a proper ancestor of $u$; a self-loop is a back edge too); black with $d[u] < d[v]$ → **forward edge** ($v$ is a descendant reached by a shortcut); black with $d[u] > d[v]$ → **cross edge** (no ancestor relation — between subtrees, or between separate trees of the forest, always pointing from a later tree to an earlier one in DFS start order).

**Undirected graphs have no forward or cross edges.** Take edge $(u,v)$ with $d[u] < d[v]$: because $v \in \mathrm{Adj}[u]$, if the edge is explored first in the $u \to v$ direction, $v$ must still be white at that moment (otherwise it would already have been explored in the $v \to u$ direction first), so it is a tree edge; if it is explored first in the $v \to u$ direction, $u$ is still gray at that time (its call has not returned yet), so it is a back edge. Either way the edge is tree or back, never forward or cross.

**Cycle detection.** A directed graph is acyclic iff its DFS has no back edge: a back edge $(u,v)$ closes the tree path $v \to \cdots \to u$ into a cycle, and conversely the first-discovered vertex $v$ on any cycle reaches the rest of the cycle by a white path, making its cycle-predecessor $u$ a descendant that closes a back edge to $v$ while $v$ is still gray. The same test works for undirected graphs provided the edge back to the immediate parent $\pi[u]$ is excluded (it is the same edge as the tree edge just descended, seen from the other side, not a real second edge in a simple graph). This is exactly how course material used alongside CENG315 argues that testing whether a connected graph is a tree lies in $\mathrm{P}$: run DFS, report NO the first time a non-parent gray neighbor appears, else YES, in $O(n+e)$.

sections.heading: Complexity and Engineering Notes
sections.body:
$$T(V, E) = \Theta(V + E)$$

Aggregate argument: DFS-VISIT runs exactly once per vertex (white → gray happens once each), contributing $\Theta(1)$ outside its loop; the loops together scan every adjacency list exactly once, and $\sum_{v} |\mathrm{Adj}[v]| = \Theta(E)$ for a digraph (each directed edge stored once) or $\Theta(E)$ for an undirected graph too, since the handshaking lemma gives $\sum_v \deg(v) = 2|E| = \Theta(E)$. Space is $\Theta(V)$ for the color/$d$/$f$/$\pi$ arrays plus up to $\Theta(V)$ recursion depth on a path-shaped graph — the reason the METU CENG213 homework that builds a DFS/BFS-based depth query over a filtered edge set explicitly asks for an iterative, stack-based version rather than relying on the call stack. Since any correct traversal must at least look at every vertex and edge once (an adversary can hide a relevant edge anywhere), $\Omega(V+E)$ is unavoidable and DFS is asymptotically optimal.

DFS's $d[]$/$f[]$ numbering is the substrate for several higher-level algorithms rather than an end in itself: sorting vertices by decreasing $f[]$ gives a topological order on a DAG; Tarjan's and Kosaraju's SCC algorithms and Hopcroft–Tarjan bridge/articulation-point detection all layer extra bookkeeping (a low-link value, or a second DFS on $G^T$) on top of the same $d[]$/$f[]$ skeleton.

complexity.notes: Aggregate bound: each vertex visited once, each adjacency list scanned once total.
Scanning row $u$ to find neighbors costs $\Theta(V)$ regardless of degree.
Acyclic iff DFS produces no back edge.
One DFS pass; output is vertices in decreasing $f[]$ order.
Two DFS passes: one on $G$ for finish order, one on $G^T$.

code.caption: Recursive DFS with timestamps and edge classification on CLRS's canonical 6-vertex example

worked_example.problem: Trace DFS on the directed graph $G=(V,E)$ with $V=\{u,v,w,x,y,z\}$ and edges $u\to v$, $u \to x$, $v \to y$, $w \to y$, $w \to z$, $x \to v$, $y \to x$, $z \to z$ (a self-loop), scanning each vertex's adjacency list and the outer loop in the fixed order $u,v,w,x,y,z$. Report every $d[]$/$f[]$ pair, classify every edge, and use the parenthesis theorem to decide whether $x$ is a descendant of $u$.
worked_example.solution:
Running the outer loop in order $u,v,w,x,y,z$:

1. `time=0`. $u$ is white → **DFS-VISIT(u)**: $d[u]=1$, color $u$ gray.
   - Scan $\mathrm{Adj}[u]=\{v,x\}$. $v$ white → tree edge $u\to v$ → **DFS-VISIT(v)**: $d[v]=2$.
     - Scan $\mathrm{Adj}[v]=\{y\}$. $y$ white → tree edge $v\to y$ → **DFS-VISIT(y)**: $d[y]=3$.
       - Scan $\mathrm{Adj}[y]=\{x\}$. $x$ white → tree edge $y\to x$ → **DFS-VISIT(x)**: $d[x]=4$.
         - Scan $\mathrm{Adj}[x]=\{v\}$. $v$ is gray → **back edge** $x\to v$.
         - $x$ finished: $f[x]=5$, black.
       - $y$ finished: $f[y]=6$, black.
     - $v$ finished: $f[v]=7$, black.
   - Back in $u$: next neighbor $x$ is black and $d[u]=1 < d[x]=4$ → **forward edge** $u\to x$.
   - $u$ finished: $f[u]=8$, black.
2. $v,x,y$ already black; outer loop moves to $w$: white → **DFS-VISIT(w)**: $d[w]=9$.
   - Scan $\mathrm{Adj}[w]=\{y,z\}$. $y$ is black and $d[w]=9 > d[y]=3$ → **cross edge** $w\to y$.
   - $z$ white → tree edge $w\to z$ → **DFS-VISIT(z)**: $d[z]=10$.
     - Scan $\mathrm{Adj}[z]=\{z\}$: $z$ itself is gray → **back edge** $z\to z$ (self-loop).
     - $z$ finished: $f[z]=11$, black.
   - $w$ finished: $f[w]=12$, black.

Final timestamps: $u{:}\,1/8$, $v{:}\,2/7$, $w{:}\,9/12$, $x{:}\,4/5$, $y{:}\,3/6$, $z{:}\,10/11$ — confirmed by compiling and running the listing above.

Edge classification: tree $\{u\to v, v\to y, y\to x, w\to z\}$; back $\{x\to v, z\to z\}$; forward $\{u\to x\}$; cross $\{w\to y\}$ — every edge gets exactly one type, and $8$ edges over $6$ vertices give $2\cdot 6=12$ timestamps ($u$ and $w$ each start their own tree, so two trees make up the forest).

Parenthesis check for $x$ vs. $u$: $[d[x],f[x]]=[4,5]$ and $[d[u],f[u]]=[1,8]$, and $4 \ge 1$, $5 \le 8$, so $[4,5]\subset[1,8]$ — by the parenthesis theorem $x$ is a descendant of $u$ (via $u \to v \to y \to x$), consistent with the forward edge $u\to x$ found directly.

pitfalls: Treating every non-tree edge found in an undirected graph as a real cycle: you must skip the tree edge back to $\pi[u]$, or every DFS on a simple undirected graph reports a false cycle.
Classifying a neighbor purely by its current color: a black neighbor can mean either forward or cross — you also need $d[u]$ vs. $d[v]$ to tell them apart.
Resetting the clock inside DFS-VISIT instead of keeping one global clock for the whole forest — this breaks the parenthesis theorem, which depends on every timestamp sharing one counter.
Assuming decreasing-$f[]$ order is a valid topological sort on any directed graph — it is only correct on a DAG; if DFS reports a back edge, no topological order exists.
Unbounded recursion on adversarial inputs such as a path-shaped or heavily skewed graph: plain recursive DFS can exhaust the call stack, which is exactly why an explicit-stack rewrite matters.
Forgetting the outer for-loop over all vertices and calling DFS-VISIT on only one starting vertex — silently ignores every other component instead of producing a full forest.
applications: Build systems and package managers detect circular dependencies with the back-edge test on the directed dependency graph before scheduling a build.
Topological sort of task graphs (spreadsheet recomputation order, compilation unit order) is a single DFS pass reading vertices off in decreasing finish time.
Kosaraju's and Tarjan's strongly-connected-components algorithms, used to find cyclic modules in call graphs, are built directly on the $d[]$/$f[]$ machinery.
Maze solving and constraint backtracking (Sudoku, N-Queens) are DFS over an implicit state graph, exploring one branch to exhaustion before backtracking.
Mark-and-sweep garbage collectors traverse the object reference graph from GC roots with a DFS- or BFS-style reachability walk to find live objects.
Compilers use DFS over control-flow graphs as the basis for dominator-tree construction and dead-code/unreachable-block elimination.
exam_focus: MIT 6.046J notes used alongside CENG315 present exactly this DFS cycle-detection test — 'is a connected graph a tree?' — as the worked example for proving a decision problem lies in P, emphasizing the $O(n+e)$ running time and the 'stop at the first back edge' termination condition; expect DFS framed as a P-membership certificate, not just as a traversal.

CENG213's THE3 assignment spec requires a DFS- or BFS-based depth query (MaxDepthViaEdgeName) over a filtered subset of edges, and explicitly notes that an iterative implementation needs an explicit stack (or a repurposed priority_queue) — METU homeworks test the iterative, non-recursive version of the traversal, not only the textbook recursive one.

self_check.question: State the white-path theorem and use it to explain, without invoking colors directly, why a directed graph is acyclic exactly when its DFS produces no back edge.
self_check.answer: White-path theorem: $v$ is a descendant of $u$ in the depth-first forest iff at time $d[u]$ there is a path from $u$ to $v$ through only white vertices. Suppose $G$ has a cycle $c$, and let $v$ be the first vertex of $c$ discovered by DFS. At time $d[v]$ every other vertex of $c$ is still white ($v$ was first), and $c$ minus $v$ is a path of white vertices from $v$ around to $v$'s predecessor $u$ on the cycle; by the white-path theorem $u$ becomes a descendant of $v$, so the tree path $v \to \cdots \to u$ exists, and the cycle's closing edge $u \to v$ is then explored while $v$ is still a proper ancestor of $u$ — a back edge. Conversely, a back edge $(u,v)$ means $v$ is an ancestor of $u$, so the tree path $v \to \cdots \to u$ together with the edge $u \to v$ is itself a cycle. So a back edge exists iff a cycle exists.

self_check.question: Using the worked example's directed graph ($u\to v, u\to x, v\to y, w\to y, w\to z, x\to v, y\to x, z\to z$, outer loop order $u,v,w,x,y,z$), is $y$ an ancestor of $w$? Justify using only the reported $d[]$/$f[]$ values, without re-deriving the trace.
self_check.answer: No. $y$'s interval is $[d[y],f[y]]=[3,6]$ and $w$'s is $[d[w],f[w]]=[9,12]$. Since $6 < 9$, the two intervals are disjoint, and by the parenthesis theorem disjoint intervals mean neither vertex is an ancestor of the other — $y$ and $w$ lie in different depth-first trees of the forest ($u$'s tree and $w$'s tree, started at different times by the outer loop), consistent with $w\to y$ being classified as a cross edge rather than a tree or back edge.

self_check.question: Design an $O(V+E)$ procedure, built on DFS, that decides whether a given undirected graph $G$ is a single tree (connected and acyclic), and argue its correctness and running time.
self_check.answer: Run one DFS-VISIT from an arbitrary start vertex $s$, and while scanning $\mathrm{Adj}[u]$ report NO the first time a gray neighbor $v$ with $v \ne \pi[u]$ is found (a back edge not to the immediate parent). If the scan finishes with no such edge, check whether the single DFS-VISIT call colored every vertex; if some vertex stayed white, output NO (disconnected), else output YES. Correctness: DFS on an undirected graph only ever produces tree or back edges, so the absence of a non-parent back edge means no cycle exists; combined with every vertex having been discovered from the single root, $G$ is connected and acyclic, i.e. a tree. Running time is $\Theta(V+E)$ by the same aggregate argument as plain DFS: one DFS-VISIT call per vertex plus one scan of each adjacency list, and the parent check adds only $O(1)$ work per edge inspection.

key_points: DFS timestamps d[v] and f[v] share one global clock across the whole forest, 2|V| values total
Parenthesis theorem: any two vertices' [d,f] intervals are nested or disjoint, never overlapping partly
White-path theorem: v is a descendant of u iff a white-only path from u to v exists at time d[u]
Undirected-graph DFS only ever produces tree and back edges — never forward or cross edges
A graph is acyclic iff its DFS produces no back edge — the standard O(V+E) cycle test
DFS runs in Θ(V+E): one DFS-VISIT call per vertex plus one scan of each adjacency list total
tagline: DFS stamps discovery/finish times whose nesting proves ancestry, classifies every edge, and detects cycles in Θ(V+E).
tldr: Depth-first search explores a graph via nested recursive calls, stamping each vertex with a discovery time $d[v]$ and finish time $f[v]$ from one shared clock. The parenthesis and white-path theorems turn these timestamps into an exact test for ancestry in the depth-first forest, and comparing a neighbor's color (and, for black neighbors, its discovery time) classifies every edge as tree, back, forward or cross. A graph is acyclic exactly when its DFS finds no back edge — the $\Theta(V+E)$ basis for cycle detection, topological sort and strongly-connected-components algorithms.
